subproblems.title: Elementary properties of the monotone C^1 cutoff
subproblems.statement: Let phi : R -> R and let eps be real with eps > 0. Assume phi is C^1, nonincreasing, phi(u) = 1 for all u <= 1 and phi(u) = 0 for all u >= 1 + eps. Write phi' := deriv phi. Then: (i) 0 <= phi(u) <= 1 for every real u; (ii) phi'(u) <= 0 for every u; (iii) phi'(u) = 0 for every u > 1 + eps; (iv) phi' is continuous; (v) there is a real C with |phi'(u)| <= C for every u.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → Antitone φ → (∀ u : ℝ, u ≤ 1 → φ u = 1) → (∀ u : ℝ, 1 + ε ≤ u → φ u = 0) → (∀ u : ℝ, 0 ≤ φ u ∧ φ u ≤ 1) ∧ (∀ u : ℝ, deriv φ u ≤ 0) ∧ (∀ u : ℝ, 1 + ε < u → deriv φ u = 0) ∧ Continuous (deriv φ) ∧ ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ u : ℝ, |deriv φ u| ≤ C
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (cutoff facts). The boundedness of phi' is made explicit because step 3(c) of the parent proof uses it.

1. Bounds on phi. Let u be real.
 - Lower bound: if u >= 1 + eps then phi(u) = 0. If u < 1 + eps then phi(u) >= phi(1 + eps) = 0, since phi is nonincreasing.
 - Upper bound: if u <= 1 then phi(u) = 1. If u > 1 then phi(u) <= phi(1) = 1.
 Hence 0 <= phi(u) <= 1. This is (i).
2. Sign of phi'. phi is nonincreasing, so every difference quotient (phi(v) - phi(u))/(v - u) with v != u is <= 0. phi is differentiable at u (it is C^1), so phi'(u) is a limit of such quotients and phi'(u) <= 0. This is (ii). In Mathlib this is Antitone.deriv_nonpos, which needs no differentiability hypothesis because deriv is 0 at points of non-differentiability.
3. Local constancy.
 - Let u > 1 + eps. The open interval (1 + eps, infinity) is a neighbourhood of u on which phi = 0. So phi agrees near u with the constant function 0, and phi'(u) = 0 (Filter.EventuallyEq.deriv_eq, deriv_const). This is (iii).
 - In the same way, for u < 1, phi = 1 on the neighbourhood (-infinity, 1) of u, so phi'(u) = 0.
4. Continuity. phi is C^1, so phi' = deriv phi is continuous (ContDiff.continuous_deriv with 1 <= 1). This is (iv).
5. Boundedness.
 - By step 3, phi'(u) = 0 whenever u < 1 or u > 1 + eps. So the support of phi' lies in the compact interval [1, 1 + eps].
 - phi' is continuous by step 4. By the extreme value theorem, |phi'| attains a maximum C on [1, 1 + eps], and C >= |phi'(1)| >= 0.
 - For u outside [1, 1 + eps], |phi'(u)| = 0 <= C. Hence |phi'(u)| <= C for every u. This is (v).
 - In Mathlib: HasCompactSupport.of_support_subset_isCompact with isCompact_Icc, then Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support, and Real.norm_eq_abs.
proof_key_steps: 0 <= phi <= 1 follows from monotonicity and the boundary values phi(1) = 1 and phi(1 + eps) = 0.
phi' <= 0 because phi is nonincreasing (Antitone.deriv_nonpos).
phi' = 0 on (1 + eps, infinity) and on (-infinity, 1), where phi is locally constant.
phi' is continuous because phi is C^1.
phi' is continuous with support in [1, 1 + eps], hence bounded by some C.

subproblems.title: Scaled L^p hypothesis: finiteness and real form on sub-balls
subproblems.statement: Let n and l be natural numbers and p real with n < p. Let mu be a measure on R^(n+l), H : R^(n+l) -> R^(n+l), y in R^(n+l), and R, Lambda, t real with R > 0, Lambda > 0 and t <= R. Write kappa := (p - n)/(4p) and, for real s, Q_s := the lower (extended) integral over the closed ball closedBall y s of |H|^p dmu, a value in [0, infinity]. Assume (ofReal(R^(p-n)) * Q_R)^(1/p) <= ofReal(kappa Lambda) in [0, infinity]. Then Q_t < infinity and (Q_t.toReal)^(1/p) <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1), with real powers.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (p : ℝ), (n : ℝ) < p → ∀ (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (H : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (R Λ t : ℝ), 0 < R → 0 < Λ → t ≤ R → (ENNReal.ofReal (R ^ (p - n)) * ∫⁻ x in closedBall y R, ‖H x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ) ^ (1 / p) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ((p - n) / (4 * p) * Λ) → ∫⁻ x in closedBall y t, ‖H x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ < ⊤ ∧ (∫⁻ x in closedBall y t, ‖H x‖ₑ ^ p ∂μ).toReal ^ (1 / p) ≤ (p - n) / (4 * p) * Λ * R ^ ((n : ℝ) / p - 1)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 2 of the parent proof (the L^p norm); Simon Ch. 4, 4.2.

0. Constants. Since p > n >= 0, p > 0 and so 1/p > 0. Also p - n > 0, kappa = (p - n)/(4p) > 0 and kappa Lambda > 0. As R > 0, c := R^(p-n) > 0, so ofReal(c) != 0.
1. Q_R is finite.
 - Suppose ofReal(c) * Q_R = infinity. Then (ofReal(c) * Q_R)^(1/p) = infinity^(1/p) = infinity, because 1/p > 0 (ENNReal.top_rpow_of_pos).
 - The hypothesis would then give infinity <= ofReal(kappa Lambda). This is impossible, since ofReal of a real number is finite. Hence ofReal(c) * Q_R != infinity.
 - If Q_R were infinity, then ofReal(c) * Q_R = ofReal(c) * infinity = infinity, because ofReal(c) != 0. So Q_R < infinity.
2. Passing to reals.
 - As Q_R < infinity, Q_R = ofReal(Q_R.toReal). Since c >= 0, ofReal(c) * Q_R = ofReal(c * Q_R.toReal).
 - Since c * Q_R.toReal >= 0 and 1/p >= 0, (ofReal(c * Q_R.toReal))^(1/p) = ofReal((c * Q_R.toReal)^(1/p)) (ENNReal.ofReal_rpow_of_nonneg).
 - Since kappa Lambda >= 0, ofReal(A) <= ofReal(kappa Lambda) is equivalent to A <= kappa Lambda (ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal_iff).
 - Hence (c * Q_R.toReal)^(1/p) <= kappa Lambda.
3. Factoring. Put N := (Q_R.toReal)^(1/p) >= 0.
 - Both factors are >= 0, so (c * Q_R.toReal)^(1/p) = c^(1/p) * N (Real.mul_rpow).
 - As R >= 0, c^(1/p) = (R^(p-n))^(1/p) = R^((p-n)(1/p)) = R^(1 - n/p) (Real.rpow_mul). Here (p - n)/p = 1 - n/p because p != 0.
 - So R^(1-n/p) * N <= kappa Lambda.
4. Dividing. R^(1-n/p) > 0, and R^(n/p - 1) = R^(-(1 - n/p)) = 1/R^(1-n/p) (Real.rpow_neg). Hence N <= kappa Lambda / R^(1-n/p) = kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1).
5. The sub-ball.
 - Since t <= R, closedBall y t is contained in closedBall y R. So Q_t <= Q_R by monotonicity of the lower integral in the domain (lintegral_mono_set). Hence Q_t < infinity.
 - toReal is monotone on finite values (ENNReal.toReal_mono, using Q_R != infinity). So 0 <= Q_t.toReal <= Q_R.toReal.
 - u -> u^(1/p) is nondecreasing on [0, infinity), as 1/p >= 0 (Real.rpow_le_rpow). Hence (Q_t.toReal)^(1/p) <= N <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1).
proof_key_steps: If ofReal(R^(p-n)) Q_R were infinite, its 1/p-th power would be infinite, contradicting the finite bound. Since ofReal(R^(p-n)) != 0, Q_R < infinity.
In real numbers the hypothesis reads (R^(p-n) Q_R.toReal)^(1/p) <= kappa Lambda.
Factor (R^(p-n))^(1/p) = R^(1 - n/p) and divide: (Q_R.toReal)^(1/p) <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1).
For t <= R, Q_t <= Q_R by set monotonicity. So Q_t < infinity and (Q_t.toReal)^(1/p) <= (Q_R.toReal)^(1/p).

subproblems.title: Hoelder absorption: |E/t^(n+1)/(1 + I/t^n)| <= 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1) (t/R)^(-n/p)
subproblems.statement: Let n >= 1 be a natural number and p, R, Lambda, eps, t, I, E, N real numbers. Assume n < p, R > 0, Lambda > 0, 0 < eps <= 1, t > 0, I >= 0 and N >= 0. Write kappa := (p - n)/(4p). Assume N <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1) and |E| <= (1 + eps) t N I^(1 - 1/p), with real powers. Then |E / t^(n+1) / (1 + I/t^n)| <= 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1) (t/R)^(-n/p). Here t^(n+1) and t^n are natural-number powers and (t/R)^(-n/p) is a real power.
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 8 of the parent proof (the bound on a); Simon Ch. 4, the estimate between 4.2 and 4.3, which uses a^(1-1/p) <= 1 + a.

0. Exponents. From 1 <= n < p we get p > 1. So gamma := 1 - 1/p satisfies 0 <= gamma <= 1. Also t^n > 0 and t^(n+1) > 0.
1. Normalized mass. Put A := I/t^n >= 0, so I = A t^n. Real powers of nonnegative numbers are multiplicative, so I^gamma = A^gamma (t^n)^gamma = A^gamma t^(n gamma) = A^gamma t^(n - n/p). This uses Real.mul_rpow, Real.rpow_natCast, Real.rpow_mul, and n gamma = n - n/p.
2. Absorption: A^gamma <= 1 + A.
 - If A <= 1, then A^gamma <= 1 <= 1 + A (Real.rpow_le_one, since 0 <= A <= 1 and gamma >= 0).
 - If A >= 1, then A^gamma <= A^1 = A <= 1 + A (Real.rpow_le_rpow_of_exponent_le, since A >= 1 and gamma <= 1).
3. Bound by 2 N t^(-n/p).
 - Put X := t N t^(n - n/p) >= 0. By the hypothesis and step 1, |E| <= (1 + eps) t N I^gamma = (1 + eps) X A^gamma.
 - Since eps <= 1 we have 1 + eps <= 2, and X A^gamma >= 0. With step 2, |E| <= 2 X A^gamma <= 2 X (1 + A).
 - As t > 0, real powers of t add: t * t^(n - n/p) = t^(1 + n - n/p) = t^(-n/p) t^(n+1). So 2 X (1 + A) = 2 N t^(-n/p) (t^(n+1) (1 + A)).
 - Since t^(n+1) > 0 and 1 + A > 0, |E / t^(n+1) / (1 + A)| = |E| / (t^(n+1) (1 + A)) <= 2 N t^(-n/p).
4. Substituting N. As t^(-n/p) > 0 and N <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1), we get 2 N t^(-n/p) <= 2 kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1) t^(-n/p).
5. Rewriting the right side.
 - Since t, R >= 0, (t/R)^(-n/p) = t^(-n/p)/R^(-n/p) = t^(-n/p) R^(n/p) (Real.div_rpow, Real.rpow_neg).
 - Since R != 0, R^(n/p - 1) = R^(n/p)/R (Real.rpow_sub_one).
 - Hence 2 kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1) t^(-n/p) = 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1) (t/R)^(-n/p).
 Since 1 + I/t^n = 1 + A, steps 3-5 give the claim. Of the hypotheses Lambda > 0 and 0 < eps <= 1, only eps <= 1 is used; the others match the calling context.
proof_key_steps: A^(1-1/p) <= 1 + A, splitting into A <= 1 and A >= 1 (0 <= 1 - 1/p <= 1 since p > 1).
Insert N <= kappa Lambda R^(n/p - 1) and rewrite R^(n/p - 1) t^(-n/p) = R^(-1) (t/R)^(-n/p).

subproblems.title: Continuity and size of the primitive G(t) = integral_0^t a
subproblems.statement: Let n be a natural number, let p, R, Lambda, eps be real numbers with n < p, R > 0, Lambda > 0 and eps > 0, and let a : R -> R. Write kappa := (p - n)/(4p) and b(t) := 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1) (t/R)^(-n/p), a real power. Assume that for every real t with t > 0 and (1 + eps) t < R, a is continuous at t and |a(t)| <= b(t). Then for every real t with t > 0 and (1 + eps) t < R: the function G(u) := integral_0^u a(tau) dtau (interval integral) is continuous at t, and |G(t)| <= Lambda/2.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (p R Λ ε : ℝ) (a : ℝ → ℝ), (n : ℝ) < p → 0 < R → 0 < Λ → 0 < ε → (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → (1 + ε) * t < R → ContinuousAt a t ∧ |a t| ≤ 2 * ((p - n) / (4 * p)) * Λ / R * (t / R) ^ (-((n : ℝ) / p))) → ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → (1 + ε) * t < R → ContinuousAt (fun u => ∫ τ in (0)..u, a τ) t ∧ |∫ τ in (0)..t, a τ| ≤ Λ / 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 10 of the parent proof (size of G); Simon Ch. 4 after 4.4, where integral_0^rho |F_0| <= (1/2) Lambda (rho/R)^(1-n/p). The continuity of G is a detail implicit in step 12 of the parent proof: there exp(-G) Q/t^n must be interval integrable on [s, r].

0. Setup.
 - Since p > n >= 0, p > 0, and beta := n/p satisfies 0 <= beta < 1.
 - Put R' := R/(1 + eps) > 0. Multiplying by 1 + eps > 0, a real tau satisfies 0 < tau < R' iff tau > 0 and (1 + eps) tau < R. So the hypothesis says: at every point of the open interval (0, R'), a is continuous and |a| <= b.
 - Fix t with t > 0 and (1 + eps) t < R, i.e. t in (0, R'). As eps > 0, t < (1 + eps) t < R, so t <= R.
1. Form of b. For tau >= 0, (tau/R)^(-beta) = tau^(-beta)/R^(-beta) (Real.div_rpow). So b(tau) = c tau^(-beta) with the constant c := 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1)/R^(-beta).
2. The bound is integrable. Since -beta > -1, tau -> tau^(-beta) is interval integrable on [0, u] for every real u (intervalIntegral.intervalIntegrable_rpow'). Hence so is tau -> c tau^(-beta).
3. a is integrable near 0. Let 0 <= u < R'.
 - The interval (0, u] is measurable and contained in (0, R'), where a is continuous. So a is a.e.-strongly measurable for Lebesgue measure restricted to (0, u] (ContinuousOn.aestronglyMeasurable).
 - For tau in (0, u], |a(tau)| <= b(tau) = c tau^(-beta), and c tau^(-beta) is integrable on (0, u] by step 2.
 - By domination (Integrable.mono'), a is integrable on (0, u], i.e. interval integrable on [0, u] (intervalIntegrable_iff_integrableOn_Ioc_of_le).
4. Continuity of G at t.
 - (0, R') is open, contains t, and a is continuous on it. So a is strongly measurable at the neighbourhood filter of t (ContinuousOn.stronglyMeasurableAtFilter).
 - By step 3 with u = t, a is interval integrable on [0, t]; and a is continuous at t.
 - By the fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right), G has derivative a(t) at t. In particular G is continuous at t.
5. Bound on G(t).
 - For every tau in (0, t], which lies in (0, R'), |a(tau)| <= c tau^(-beta). The right side is interval integrable on [0, t] by step 2.
 - Hence |G(t)| <= integral_0^t c tau^(-beta) dtau (intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le, with 0 <= t).
 - By the power rule integral_rpow (valid as -beta > -1) and 0^(1-beta) = 0 (as 1 - beta > 0), this integral is c (t^(1-beta) - 0^(1-beta))/(1 - beta) = c t^(1-beta)/(1 - beta).
6. Evaluation.
 - R^(-beta) R = R^(1-beta) (Real.rpow_add_one), so c = 2 kappa Lambda / R^(1-beta). Hence c t^(1-beta)/(1 - beta) = (2 kappa/(1 - beta)) Lambda t^(1-beta)/R^(1-beta).
 - Since p != 0 and p - n != 0, 2 kappa/(1 - beta) = 2 ((p - n)/(4p)) (p/(p - n)) = 1/2.
 - Since 0 < t <= R and 1 - beta > 0, t^(1-beta) <= R^(1-beta) (Real.rpow_le_rpow). As R^(1-beta) > 0, t^(1-beta)/R^(1-beta) <= 1.
 - With Lambda > 0, |G(t)| <= (Lambda/2) t^(1-beta)/R^(1-beta) <= Lambda/2.
proof_key_steps: On (0, R/(1+eps)), a is continuous and |a(tau)| <= c tau^(-n/p), with c = 2 kappa Lambda R^(-1) R^(n/p).
tau^(-n/p) is integrable near 0 since -n/p > -1. So a is interval integrable on [0, u] for every u < R/(1+eps).
FTC at t (a is continuous at t and strongly measurable near t): G has derivative a(t), so G is continuous at t.
|G(t)| <= integral_0^t c tau^(-n/p) = c t^(1-n/p)/(1-n/p) = (Lambda/2) (t/R)^(1-n/p) <= Lambda/2, using 2 kappa/(1 - n/p) = 1/2 and t <= R.

subproblems.title: Integrability of the test integrands on interior closed balls
subproblems.statement: Let n and l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), H : R^(n+l) -> R^(n+l), w : R^(n+l) -> R, y in R^(n+l), and R, S real with S < R. Assume mu(closedBall y R) < infinity, H is mu-integrable on closedBall y R, w is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to the open ball ball y R, and 0 <= w(x) <= 1 for mu-a.e. x in ball y R. Then the constant function 1, the function x -> (x - y).H(x) (real inner product) and w are all mu-integrable on closedBall y S.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (H : Amb n ℓ → Amb n ℓ) (w : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (R S : ℝ), S < R → μ (closedBall y R) < ⊤ → IntegrableOn H (closedBall y R) μ → AEStronglyMeasurable w (μ.restrict (ball y R)) → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, x ∈ ball y R → 0 ≤ w x ∧ w x ≤ 1) → IntegrableOn (fun _ => (1 : ℝ)) (closedBall y S) μ ∧ IntegrableOn (fun x => inner ℝ (x - y) (H x)) (closedBall y S) μ ∧ IntegrableOn w (closedBall y S) μ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 3(a) and 3(b) of the parent proof (integrability). They supply the integrability hypothesis of cutoff_calculus for f = 1, (x - y).H and w.

1. Inclusions. If ||x - y|| <= S then ||x - y|| < R. So closedBall y S is contained in ball y R (closedBall_subset_ball), which is contained in closedBall y R (ball_subset_closedBall). Directly, closedBall y S is contained in closedBall y R by closedBall_subset_closedBall, since S <= R. Hence mu(closedBall y S) <= mu(closedBall y R) < infinity.
2. The constant 1. A constant function is integrable on a set of finite measure (integrableOn_const). So 1 is integrable on closedBall y S.
3. The pairing.
 - H is integrable on closedBall y S, by restricting its integrability on the larger set closedBall y R (IntegrableOn.mono_set).
 - The map x -> x - y is continuous, H is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to closedBall y S, and (u, v) -> <u, v> is continuous. Hence x -> <x - y, H(x)> is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to closedBall y S (Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable₂ applied to continuous_inner). AEStronglyMeasurable.inner is not in the import closure of GMT.Ch05.Submission, so this route is the one to use.
 - For x in closedBall y S, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives |<x - y, H(x)>| <= ||x - y|| ||H(x)|| <= R ||H(x)||, because ||x - y|| <= S < R.
 - x -> R ||H(x)|| is integrable on closedBall y S. By domination (Integrable.mono', with the a.e. bound for the restricted measure via ae_restrict_iff'), the pairing is integrable on closedBall y S.
4. The weight.
 - closedBall y S is contained in ball y R. So mu restricted to closedBall y S is at most mu restricted to ball y R, and w is a.e.-strongly measurable for the former (AEStronglyMeasurable.mono_measure with Measure.restrict_mono).
 - This restricted measure is finite by step 1.
 - For mu-a.e. x in closedBall y S we have x in ball y R, hence 0 <= w(x) <= 1 and |w(x)| <= 1.
 - So w is dominated a.e. by the integrable constant 1, and it is integrable on closedBall y S.
proof_key_steps: S < R gives closedBall y S within ball y R within closedBall y R, so mu(closedBall y S) < infinity.
Constants are integrable on sets of finite measure.
<x - y, H(x)> is a.e.-strongly measurable and bounded by R |H(x)| on closedBall y S; it is dominated by the integrable R |H|.
w is a.e.-strongly measurable on closedBall y S with |w| <= 1 a.e. there; it is dominated by 1 on a finite measure.

subproblems.title: Splitting the radial first-variation integrand, with the signs of its parts
subproblems.statement: Let n and l be natural numbers, mu a measure on R^(n+l), w : R^(n+l) -> R, y in R^(n+l), R and eps real, and phi : R -> R. Assume eps > 0; mu(closedBall y R) < infinity; w is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to the open ball ball y R, and 0 <= w(x) <= 1 for mu-a.e. x in ball y R; phi is C^1 and nonincreasing, with phi(u) = 1 for u <= 1 and phi(u) = 0 for u >= 1 + eps. Let t be real with t > 0 and (1 + eps) t < R. Write r_x := |x - y| and phi' := deriv phi; all integrals are Bochner integrals over R^(n+l) with respect to mu. Then: (a) integral (n phi(r_x/t) + (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t)(1 - w(x))) dmu = n integral phi(r_x/t) dmu + integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) dmu - integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) w(x) dmu; (b) integral phi(r_x/t) dmu >= 0; (c) integral (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) w(x) dmu <= 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Amb n ℓ)) (w : Amb n ℓ → ℝ) (y : Amb n ℓ) (R ε : ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ), 0 < ε → μ (closedBall y R) < ⊤ → AEStronglyMeasurable w (μ.restrict (ball y R)) → (∀ᵐ x ∂μ, x ∈ ball y R → 0 ≤ w x ∧ w x ≤ 1) → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → Antitone φ → (∀ u : ℝ, u ≤ 1 → φ u = 1) → (∀ u : ℝ, 1 + ε ≤ u → φ u = 0) → ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → (1 + ε) * t < R → ∫ x, ((n : ℝ) * φ (‖x - y‖ / t) + ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * (1 - w x)) ∂μ = (n : ℝ) * ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / t) ∂μ + ∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) ∂μ - ∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * w x ∂μ ∧ 0 ≤ ∫ x, φ (‖x - y‖ / t) ∂μ ∧ ∫ x, ‖x - y‖ / t * deriv φ (‖x - y‖ / t) * w x ∂μ ≤ 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 3(c), the first two bullets of step 5, and step 6 of the parent proof. Uses the sibling lemma cutoff_facts.

1. Cutoff facts. Apply cutoff_facts to phi and eps; its hypotheses are among ours. It gives:
 - 0 <= phi <= 1 and phi' <= 0 everywhere;
 - phi'(u) = 0 for u > 1 + eps;
 - phi' is continuous;
 - |phi'(u)| <= C for all u, for some real C. Necessarily C >= |phi'(0)| >= 0.
2. Geometry. Let B := closedBall y ((1 + eps) t).
 - As (1 + eps) t < R, B is contained in ball y R, which is contained in closedBall y R. So mu(B) < infinity.
 - For every x, r_x/t >= 0.
 - If x is in B, then r_x <= (1 + eps) t, so r_x/t <= 1 + eps. If x is not in B, then r_x > (1 + eps) t, so r_x/t > 1 + eps (as t > 0).
3. The three integrands. Put f1(x) := phi(r_x/t), f2(x) := (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) and f3(x) := f2(x) w(x).
 - x -> r_x/t is continuous, and phi and phi' are continuous. So f1 and f2 are continuous, hence a.e.-strongly measurable.
 - If x is not in B, then r_x/t > 1 + eps. So f1(x) = phi(r_x/t) = 0, and phi'(r_x/t) = 0, hence f2(x) = f3(x) = 0. Thus f1, f2 and f3 vanish outside B.
4. Integrability.
 (i) |f1| <= 1 everywhere. So f1 is integrable on B: it is bounded and a.e.-strongly measurable on a set of finite measure (Measure.integrableOn_of_bounded). As f1 vanishes off B, it is mu-integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero).
 (ii) For x in B, |f2(x)| = (r_x/t) |phi'(r_x/t)| <= (1 + eps) C. So f2 is integrable on B, and as it vanishes off B it is mu-integrable.
 (iii) Since B is contained in ball y R, w is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to B, by restriction to a smaller set. So the product f3 = f2 w is a.e.-strongly measurable for mu restricted to B.
  - For mu-a.e. x in B we have x in ball y R. Hence 0 <= w(x) <= 1 and |f3(x)| = |f2(x)| w(x) <= |f2(x)| <= (1 + eps) C.
  - mu restricted to B is finite, so f3 is integrable on B by domination by a constant (Integrable.mono'). As it vanishes off B, it is mu-integrable.
5. The splitting identity (a).
 - For every x, n phi(r_x/t) + (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t)(1 - w(x)) = n f1(x) + f2(x) - f3(x).
 - By step 4 and linearity of the Bochner integral (integral_sub, integral_add, integral_const_mul), integral (n f1 + f2 - f3) dmu = n integral f1 dmu + integral f2 dmu - integral f3 dmu.
 This is (a).
6. Nonnegativity (b). f1 >= 0 everywhere because phi >= 0. So integral f1 dmu >= 0 (integral_nonneg).
7. Sign of the w-term (c). f3 <= 0 mu-a.e. Indeed, for mu-a.e. x:
 - if x is in ball y R, then w(x) >= 0, and f2(x) = (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) <= 0 because r_x/t >= 0 and phi' <= 0; so f3(x) = f2(x) w(x) <= 0;
 - if x is not in ball y R, then x is not in B (as B is contained in ball y R), so f3(x) = 0 by step 3.
 Hence integral f3 dmu <= 0 (integral_nonpos_of_ae).
proof_key_steps: cutoff_facts gives 0 <= phi <= 1, phi' <= 0, phi' = 0 on (1 + eps, infinity), and phi' continuous and bounded by C.
B := closedBall y ((1 + eps) t) lies in ball y R and has finite measure, and r_x/t > 1 + eps off B.
phi(r_x/t), (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) and (r_x/t) phi'(r_x/t) w(x) vanish off B and are bounded and a.e.-strongly measurable on B, hence mu-integrable.
Linearity splits the radial integrand into n times the integral of phi(r_x/t), plus the integral of (r_x/t) phi', minus the integral of (r_x/t) phi' w.
phi >= 0 makes the integral of phi(r_x/t) nonnegative; (r_x/t) phi' w <= 0 a.e. makes the w-term nonpositive.
